items.title: Lawrence Duhé Interview, 1957-06-09
items.q: Sugar Johnny, Louie Kepard on the guitar, Roy Palmer, Herbert Lindsay, Eddie Garland, and Toby Hall on the drums.

ctx.x: He had a big tone, most people say. Oh, it was a much more powerful man, but that style. That style, mm-hmm. When you went to Chicago, what was that date that tells here on this contract? That's April 1917. That's correct. Who all was in that band?
Sugar Johnny, Louie Kepard on the guitar, Roy Palmer, Herbert Lindsay, Eddie Garland, and Toby Hall on the drums.

items.title: Roy Palmer Interview, 1955-09-22
items.q: The clarinetist was this fellow, Dewey, Lawrence Dewey. He played a C clarinet.

ctx.x: This is Roy Palmer speaking, and I want to say about the bands, different bands that we have played with in the Orleans and in different towns, different places. I want to explain how I came along in the music game. It was when I was around 15 or 18, I studied music, taking music. From that time I was taking bands, taking bands. I played with regular, and sometimes I played with other bands. I led a lot of bands, bass band and so on. My music was well established because I played and I played with other bands. I…

a very good band. What did they pay in the parades? In the parades they paid two dollars an hour. Yes, two dollars an hour. They only paraded about two hours and a half. We only made about four or five hours on the parade. We had so many different, and then through Connerville, and like those days, well we got hired. We had to play probably six or eight hours we played, see? Or eight or ten hours at night, see? For dances? Yeah, for dances, see? Different places at the fairground and at the Louisiana Park, and…
